planting.note: Divide clumps after flowering in cool weather for best establishment.

directions: A long-cultivated miniature polyanthus type forming tight rosettes that cover themselves in pale primrose-yellow flowers on short stems in early spring. It stays compact and tidy without deadheading, making it a reliable edger under deciduous shrubs or at the front of a woodland bed. Give it humus-rich, evenly moist soil and dappled light; it resents hot, dry summer sites. Established clumps benefit from division every few years to keep flowering vigorous.

planting.note: Best moved as container divisions rather than from seed, since the novelty flower form does not come reliably true.

directions: A novelty English primrose grown for frilly, ruffled petals in an unusual celadon-green shade around a small yellow eye, rather than for a conventional flower color. It forms a low rosette of crinkled leaves typical of the species and flowers heavily in early spring before easing off in summer heat. Plant it in cool, humus-rich soil in a woodland border where it will not be baked by afternoon sun. Divide congested clumps every two to three years to keep the odd green blooms coming reliably.

planting.note: Evergreen rosettes can also be divided in early fall in milder zones.

directions: A soft-flowered pigsqueak selection that sends up dense clusters of pale pink bells on red stems well above the rounded, leathery leaf mounds in mid spring. The glossy foliage picks up red and bronze tones once cold weather arrives, giving the clump a second season of interest. It tolerates a wide range of soils but looks its best with consistent moisture and light shade from hot afternoon sun. Slugs can disfigure the leaves, so keep an eye on new growth in damp seasons.

planting.note: A compact selection; divide congested crowns in spring.

directions: A compact pigsqueak selection (its name means 'winter fairy tale') with loose heads of pale pink flowers fading to white held just above a tight rosette of rounded, leathery leaves. The leaves are its real draw in the off-season, turning a vivid scarlet-red through winter instead of the duller bronze typical of many Bergenia cultivars. Its smaller stature suits the front of a shaded border or a container, where the bold winter leaf color reads well against evergreen ferns. Plant in humus-rich soil with reliable moisture; it tolerates cold well but sulks through prolonged summer drought.

planting.note: Divide clumps every 3-4 years to maintain bloom density.

directions: One of the latest-blooming astilbes available, holding off its soft mauve-pink plumes until late summer when most other astilbes have already finished. The compact, well-branched habit and fine-textured foliage make it useful for extending color in a shaded perennial bed into early fall. It needs consistently moist, rich soil and will scorch at the leaf edges if allowed to dry out during bloom. Combine it with later ferns or hostas to carry interest through the season's end.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to sun.

directions: A selection of the native Ozark witch hazel grown for two distinct seasonal displays: slender, ribbon-like copper-red flowers that open along bare stems in late winter, followed months later by a fall foliage show of yellow, orange, and red that gives the cultivar its name. It forms a rounded, multi-stemmed shrub that tolerates the periodic wet, gravelly streambank conditions of its native range and adapts well to woodland-edge plantings with light to moderate shade. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape, and expect a slow-to-moderate grower that needs several seasons to reach full size.

planting.note: Site in moist, well-drained, acidic soil with an open spot so the cascading form can be seen from below.

directions: Selected in the Netherlands by Pierre Lombarts Nursery in the 1940s, this vernal witch hazel stands apart for its distinctly weeping, spreading branch structure, which carries the same lightly scented, thread-like orange-red and yellow flowers in late winter but displays them along cascading rather than upright stems. It develops mid-green summer foliage that turns yellow or purplish in fall depending on soil chemistry, and performs best in open, acidic, well-drained ground rather than shallow or chalky sites. Its horizontal, fountain-like habit makes it a useful specimen for underplanting with shade perennials where its form can be appreciated from above.

planting.note: Give it room to form a multi-stemmed colony, since this vigorous, suckering selection spreads over time in favorable sites.

directions: Named by Hillier Nursery in England in 1966 for its unusually saturated reddish-orange, strap-like winter flowers, this vigorous, vase-shaped shrub was selected from the native Ozark witch hazel and is one of the reddest-flowered selections of the species. Flowers open on bare branches in late winter, ahead of most other shrubs, and are followed by clean, disease-free foliage that colors well in fall. Over time it can sucker and form a loose colony, which makes it useful as an informal woodland-edge mass but something to plan for when siting. It takes a few years to reach full size and asks for little beyond moist, acidic soil and light shaping after bloom.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil that stays evenly moist; well suited to shaded terrace containers and woodland-garden borders where its colorful new growth is visible at eye level.

directions: A compact, mound-forming evergreen bred by Ron van Opstal in the Netherlands, grown for new growth that emerges deep orange-brown before deepening to burgundy in autumn, with repeat flushes of color through the growing season. Its dense, gracefully arching stems and slow growth rate suit small shaded borders and foundation plantings where a full-size leucothoe would be too large. It carries small, bell-shaped white spring flowers typical of the species but is grown chiefly for its colorful evergreen foliage. Give it consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a shaded to partly shaded spot, since full sun and dry soil stress the foliage.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to consistently moist, acidic soil in partial shade; tolerates occasional flooding, suiting rain gardens or shaded streamside plantings.

directions: This selected form of the native downy American snowbell is distinguished from the typical species by new growth and foliage carrying a soft silvery-blue cast, a trait inherited from its pubescent-leaved botanical variety. Like the species, it bears nodding, white, reflexed flowers with prominent yellow stamens along arching stems in late spring, and the variety is native to wet pine flatwoods and wet woods from South Carolina to Florida and Texas, making it well adapted to humid, moisture-retentive garden soils. It remains uncommon in the nursery trade compared to Japanese snowbell, which makes it a worthwhile choice for gardeners wanting a regionally native alternative with ornamental foliage interest. Site it where soil stays reliably moist and shade is partial rather than deep, since flowering is reduced in heavy shade.

planting.note: Plant container stock in part shade in spring; propagate by division or softwood cuttings to keep the double-flowered trait true, since seedlings revert to single flowers.

directions: This thornless thimbleberry selection was found around 1975 on Starrett Hill near Monte Rio, California, and named for a Sonoma State University art instructor; it carries extra petals on its blossoms instead of the species' usual flat white flower. Despite the showier bloom it still sets the typical soft, thimble-shaped fruit, described by growers as mild and sweet and readily taken by birds. Its large, downy, maple-like leaves and suckering habit make it a good choice for naturalizing a shaded woodland edge or screening a partly shaded slope. Keep the soil evenly moist, since thimbleberry foliage scorches quickly if it dries out in a sunnier spot.

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring or early fall into acidic, humus-rich soil in dappled shade beneath shrubs or conifers.

directions: Cherry Berries was selected for carrying noticeably larger, more numerous cherry-red fruit than wild wintergreen, with berries persisting from fall through spring on a low evergreen mat. The glossy foliage deepens to a merlot shade once cold weather sets in, then greens back up in spring alongside small white bell flowers. It spreads faster and tolerates a wider range of soils than straight-species wintergreen, though it still wants the acidic, well-drained conditions typical of an Ericaceae understory planting. The mildly wintergreen-flavored berries are edible fresh or steeped for tea, and persistent fruit also draws birds through the winter months.

planting.note: Plant in dappled to full shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil; grows slowly at first but fills in as a dense mat over a few seasons.

directions: Introduced by Jelitto Perennial Seeds in Germany in 2014, this wintergreen selection was chosen for vigor and heavy fruit set, carrying light pink spring flowers followed by unusually large, bright red berries that hold on the plant from autumn into spring. The glossy evergreen leaves turn a deep merlot color in cold weather, giving the low mat year-round interest even without fruit showing. Berries have the grainy texture and faint wintergreen flavor typical of the species and are edible, though better nibbled fresh than eaten in quantity. It grows more slowly and compactly than some wintergreen selections, making it well suited to a shaded rock garden edge or woodland groundcover border.

planting.note: Start the fine seed indoors on the soil surface under light, keep evenly moist, and transplant into part-shade beds after the last frost.

directions: Attila stands out among alpine strawberries for throwing runners fairly freely, more like a conventional garden strawberry than the tight, runnerless clumps typical of this type. It still delivers the small, intensely perfumed red fruit prized in alpine strawberries, bearing from its first summer and continuing from June into fall. Because the plants spread modestly on their own, Attila fills in faster as a low edible groundcover beneath open shrubs or at the shaded edge of a border than clump-forming alpine types. Give it humus-rich, evenly moist soil and morning sun to light afternoon shade for the steadiest fruit set.

planting.note: Start seed indoors on the soil surface under light and transplant runnerless clumps into part-shade beds after the last frost.

directions: This white-fruited sport of the old German 'Baron Solemacher' alpine strawberry produces pale, cream-colored berries that are among the largest of the white alpine types, with a wild-strawberry aroma carrying a faint pineapple note. Plants stay in tidy, runnerless clumps and bear day-neutral through the growing season rather than in one main flush. Because the ripe fruit never turns the red that birds key in on, White Solemacher often escapes bird damage better than red-fruited alpine strawberries planted in the same partly shaded bed. It makes a neat edible edging for a shaded path or the dappled margin of a woodland garden.

planting.note: Start seed indoors on the soil surface under light and transplant into part-shade beds of humus-rich soil after the last frost.

directions: Bowlenzauber (German for roughly 'punch bowl magic') is an older German alpine strawberry selection bred for scarlet fruit with an unusually concentrated, wine-like sweetness, originally intended for flavoring fruit punches and desserts. Like most alpine strawberries it stays in a compact, day-neutral-fruiting clump with few runners, making it easy to tuck into a partly shaded bed without it wandering. It bears over a long season rather than one big flush, giving a steady trickle of small, highly aromatic berries from late spring into fall. Morning sun with afternoon shade and consistently moist, rich soil keep it fruiting without scorching the foliage.
